sentences.text: Unlike its relatives, this dinosaur was bulkier and more robust in build.
It reached a length of 11.6 meters and weighed between 6 and 7.4 metric tons.
Its teeth were chisel-like with wrinkled enamel, heavy serrations, and laterally flattened crowns.
The estimated skull length is 1.22 meters.
Unlike other carcharodontosaurids, it lacked pneumatic foramina extending into the sacral and caudal vertebrae.
It possessed a fused and highly developed scapulocoracoid while retaining very small forelimbs.
Its teeth were less lamellar than relatives and featured unique denticle structures with a central groove.
The proximal caudal vertebrae had an exceptionally high neural spine, approximately twice the size of the vertebral centrum.
Tyrannotitan chubutensis was described by Fernando E. Novas, Silvina de Valais, Pat Vickers-Rich, and Tom Rich in 2005.
The only known species is represented by two fossil specimens found 400 meters apart by technicians Pablo Puerta and Leandro Guerrero.
Fossils were found at La Juanita Farm, 28 km northeast of Paso de Indios, Chubut Province, Argentina.
Evidence suggests Tyrannotitan was an active hunter using a powerful bite, though it may have also scavenged opportunistically.
Broken teeth found in the same rock layer as a giant sauropod suggest that Tyrannotitan acted as a scavenger, breaking its own teeth while tearing tough skin.
Fossil evidence suggests that Tyrannotitan persisted for millions of years after the death of the original two specimens found.
Tyrannotitan belongs to the tribe Giganotosaurini.
Canale et al. (2022) placed Tyrannotitan within the clade Giganotosaurini, alongside Meraxes, Giganotosaurus, and Mapusaurus.

It shares specific anatomical traits with Mapusaurus and Giganotosaurus, including a wide postorbital process on the jugal, absence of pleurocoels in caudal vertebrae, and a reduced fourth trochanter on the femur.
Because Tyrannotitan skull remains are extremely incomplete, its head shape is reconstructed based on general family characteristics rather than direct evidence.
Tyrannotitan lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.
The Paleobiology Database records the time range of Tyrannotitan as the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 100.5 million years ago.
It is debated whether significant differences between Tyrannotitan and related taxa are due to evolution or sexual dimorphism, though the latter seems unlikely.
